name: Air Superiority Blue
lede: Air Superiority Blue is a muted sky blue named for the military doctrine of controlling the air over a battlefield, standardized on United States Federal Standard 595 paint chips.

sections.title: A military paint chip
sections.body:
"Air superiority" is a doctrine term for one side controlling the skies over a battle, and the color takes its name from paint used on aircraft under that doctrine [1]. Wikipedia traces the name to Federal Standard 595, the United States government's paint-chip standard for military equipment, rather than to any older dictionary [1]. No earlier record turns up in the pigment and color-name books consulted here, so the word's exact coining date is undocumented [1].

That gap between a military paint standard and a dictionary entry is typical of newer color names: they arrive through industry catalogs and style guides rather than through the pigment and dye trade that produced older names [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this blue in 138 of 23,781 paintings (0.58 percent, as photographed), more common than 58 percent of named colors here [2]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 1.4 times the expected rate for that century [2]. Alfred Sisley is its most devoted painter, using it in 5 of his 50 works here, nearly seven times the rate of the museums his paintings come from [2]. The earliest matching canvas dates to 1482, nearly four centuries before the name existed; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and a look-alike hue, not a sign the paint itself is old [2]. It is most over-represented in French paintings, at 2.3 times the expected share [2]. The nearest named look-alikes are [[iceberg]] and [[carolina-blue]], with [[grey-blue]] and [[squill-blue]] a little further off [3]. None of that painting-archive presence has anything to do with the Air Force: it simply shows that muted sky blues of this kind recur across centuries of landscape and portrait painting [2].

questions.q: Where does the name "Air Superiority Blue" come from?
True or false: finding this blue in a painting from 1482 proves the color existed under this name then.

openers: This sky blue's name comes from a military paint chip, not a dictionary.

issues: Exact coining date undocumented; stated as such rather than guessed.
